params.text: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers.
Rows run across; columns run down.
This example has 2 rows and 3 columns: a 2 by 3 matrix.
A spreadsheet, a pixel grid, and a table of measurements are all matrix-shaped.
Each position has a meaning set by its row and column.
Matrices can be added when they have the same shape.
Add each number to the number in the same position.
Multiplying a matrix by a number scales every entry.
Matrix multiplication combines rows of the first matrix with columns of the second.
Multiply matching entries, then add the products.
A 2 by 3 matrix times a 3 by 1 matrix gives a 2 by 1 matrix.
The inside dimensions must match; the outside dimensions give the answer's shape.
A matrix can transform a vector: rotate, stretch, reflect, or shear it.
For a quarter-turn, (x, y) becomes (-y, x).
Multiplying two transformation matrices combines their actions.

point  →  rotate  →  stretch
       same as one combined matrix
Matrices organize numbers so operations can act on many values at once.
Know the shape. Match positions. For multiplication, pair rows with columns.

subtitles.text: Think of a matrix as a compact way to store relationships.
The entry in row 2, column 3 is 5. We write that position as b₂₃.
For an image, each cell can store a pixel value. For data, it can store a measurement.
Here, top left is 1 plus 4, and bottom right is 1 plus 6.
A scalar changes the values while keeping the same rows and columns.
The result is one number: the dot product of that row and column.
If the inside numbers do not match, that multiplication is not defined.
Apply this matrix to (2, 1), and the point moves to (-1, 2).
This lets graphics and robotics build complex motion from simple steps.
You now know how to read a matrix, add and scale one, multiply matrices, and use them to transform space.
